current_answer: A new U.S. check finds no statistically significant summer-2026 unemployment spike among recent college graduates relative to earlier summers, older graduates or young adults without a college degree. That blocks a clean national “AI has made graduates unemployed” headline. It does not clear the entry-level risk: other U.S. studies find weaker initial employment, earnings or postings in more AI-exposed work. Those sources measure different cohorts and outcomes, not a common AI-adoption experiment. The evidence now says the entry problem is real enough to watch, but too mixed to call a national AI unemployment verdict for your career.

catalogue_card.question: Did AI cause a national graduate unemployment spike?
catalogue_card.text: Not in a new summer-2026 CPS check. That result cannot erase separate warnings about initial jobs, pay or local postings.

summary: A September 2026 IZA discussion paper using U.S. CPS microdata finds no statistically significant summer-2026 relative unemployment increase among recent college graduates, whether it compares them with earlier summers, older graduates or young adults without a college degree.
The result remains null when the authors include “sidelined unemployed,” so the finding is not only a narrow unemployment-definition artifact in that paper.

The paper does not observe employer AI adoption. In occupation interactions, it finds some evidence that remote-work availability, rather than AI exposure alone, is positively related to 2026 unemployment.

A Census administrative-record study still finds lower initial employment and earnings for graduates in the most AI-exposed majors after ChatGPT. Initial job matches and summer unemployment are different outcomes; neither study settles the other.
Texas posting evidence and the broad U.S. posting counter-signal remain relevant, but neither is a count of recent-graduate unemployment or a personal forecast.
uncertainty: The new CPS result covers a short summer window and relative unemployment comparisons; it does not measure an employer’s generative-AI adoption, first-job quality, earnings or vacancies.
The Census graduate study and the CPS study use different cohorts, data, periods, outcomes and comparison groups. Their contrast does not identify the cause of either pattern.
U.S. early-career findings remain largely exposure-based. Remote work, education, pre-trends, other shocks and sample selection remain live attribution problems.
No current study can tell a reader whether their own job will be lost to AI.
freshness_note: Updated 18 September 2026 after a new U.S. CPS analysis found no statistically significant summer unemployment spike among recent college graduates. We will revise when a common design follows the same cohorts from search through first job, earnings and later employment while observing employer AI adoption.
